paras: The posse pursuit of Gus Epps took place near Huntington, West Virginia, on July 19, 1903, when about twenty armed young men chased Epps, a Black man accused of stabbing William Vinson, and fired an estimated fifty shots at him. A wire dispatch reported that Epps drowned under fire in Twelve Pole river, and one Illinois paper headed the story "Mob Kills Another Negro." Local papers reported instead that he escaped across the creek, was arrested in Ironton, Ohio, that night, and was later sentenced to two years in the state penitentiary.

According to the Huntington Advertiser, Vinson, a young man from Catlettsburg, Kentucky, was stabbed in an alley on Eighth street at about half-past one on the night of Saturday, July 18. Vinson's companions said a white boy had knocked Epps down in a street quarrel minutes earlier, and that Epps, perhaps taking Vinson for that boy, then struck him in the breast with a knife. The West Virginia News said instead that three white men had assaulted Epps outside the Huntington Hotel and that he stabbed Vinson, thinking him one of them.

Vinson's friends and a police lieutenant, Sam Davis, chased Epps up Eighth street, but he got away. As news of the stabbing spread, the Advertiser reported, "there was talk of a lynching if the negro could be found." At five o'clock Sunday morning a posse of about twenty "well armed" young men took the streetcar toward Kenova, expecting Epps to try to catch a train there. Passing Camden park, members who knew Epps saw him in a field, stopped the car, and chased him toward Twelve Pole creek.

The Advertiser estimated that "no less than fifty shots" were fired at Epps as he ran into the bushes; he fell several times and was thought to be wounded. He crossed the creek in a boat out of pistol range, and the posse lost him; a Catlettsburg party later searched several miles into Ohio.

Early Sunday night the Ironton chief of police arrested Epps as he tried to board a freight train, and on July 20 Huntington's police chief, Morris Davis, brought him back to the Cabell county jail. The Louisville Courier-Journal's correspondent wrote that when Epps arrived "many threats were made" and he was "quickly hustled behind the bars."

Vinson was taken home to Catlettsburg, and by the end of July he was reported to be improving and out of danger. Epps was charged with assault with intent to kill; his preliminary hearing was postponed from July 31 to August 8 at the state's request. On November 20 the Advertiser reported that he had been sentenced to two years in the state penitentiary, the minimum for the offense.

The Huntington Advertiser put the case on its front page on July 20, under a headline saying the "fleeing negro" had escaped amid "showers of bullets," and followed it through the postponed hearing and the sentence. The Courier-Journal's special dispatch called the stabbing an "unwarranted assault" and described Vinson's friends as "greatly enraged."

A wire dispatch dated July 19 said instead that Vinson had been "fatally stabbed" and that Epps, "badly injured" by the posse's shots, drowned trying to swim the river. Papers in Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana and Mississippi reprinted it into August under headings such as "Swimming Negro Used as Target," "Drowned While Fleeing from a Posse" and "Negro Fugitive Drowned." The Rock Island Argus replaced "posse" with "mob" throughout and headed the item "Mob Kills Another Negro." As late as July 25 the West Virginia News, under the head "Killed by Mistake," said Epps "sank to a watery grave."

The Ceredo Advance printed the drowning story on July 22 and, on August 5, reported Epps awaiting a hearing without remarking on the earlier item. All of the coverage came from white papers; no Black-press account of the episode appears among the sources.

The wire dispatch and the West Virginia News said Epps drowned under fire, while the Advertiser and the Courier-Journal reported his arrest at Ironton the same day. The local reports are the better evidence: they name the arresting officers and the jail, and later reports follow his hearing and sentence.

reader.title: Posse pursuit of Gus Epps
bases: An armed party of about twenty young men chased Epps after he was accused of stabbing Vinson and fired an estimated fifty shots at him, but he escaped and was later arrested by police, so no one was killed (A2, A7, A18).

A posse of about twenty fired on Epps as a fugitive accused of stabbing Vinson, and there was 'talk of a lynching', but he escaped across Twelve Pole creek and was arrested at Ironton, jailed and later sentenced (A2, A7, A18); the wire report that he drowned under fire (A3, A12) is contradicted by the local reports.

The stabbing, the armed posse's pursuit and the shooting at Epps are reported independently by the Huntington Advertiser, a Courier-Journal special and the wire dispatch (A2, A7, A3), though they disagree on whether Epps survived.

framing.detail: The Huntington Advertiser called the cutting 'entirely without provocation' and reported talk of lynching without comment, while also printing that a white boy had knocked Epps down first.
The Courier-Journal special called it an 'unwarranted assault' and reported Vinson's friends 'greatly enraged' and the threats against Epps.
Wire papers carried the drowning version under heads such as 'Drowned Trying to Escape' and 'Swimming Negro Used as Target'.
The Rock Island Argus substituted 'mob' for 'posse' and headed the item 'Mob Kills Another Negro'.
